newsitem.title: USA: Economists see big benefits in power deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Economists see big benefits in power deregulation.

text.p: Pointing to consumer gains in five deregulated industries similar to the power industry, two economists said Tuesday that electricity markets should be opened to competition rapidly.

With federal lawmakers poised to begin debating whether to force states to break up utility monopolies over retail power supplies, the two economists looked at the consumer impact of deregulation in the natural gas, telecommunications, airlines,
trucking, and railroad industries as a guide.
Within 10 years of deregulation in those industries, prices to consumers fell by at least 25 percent, they said.
In all five of those industries, customers and suppliers are linked by some type of network, as is the case in the power industry.

"In every case, deregulation has worked," said Robert Crandall of the Brookings Institution, one of the authors of the report. "Competition induces change, lower service costs," he said at a news conference.
Jerry Ellig of George Mason University's Center for Market Processes dismissed concerns that rural communities might lose electricity service if utilities are no longer required to serve them.
Looking at the airline industry, he said that most of the 100 to 200 communities which had lost air service since 1978 could not blame deregulation for the loss.
Those communities had been receiving unregulated service even before the industry was overhauled, said Ellig, the second author of the report.
If anything, he said, innovations such as commuter airlines had improved service to smaller communities.
Crandall similarly dismissed concern that utilities would reconsolidate, stifling competition, once the new market settled down.

"I'm not too concerned we're ever going to see enough consolidation to eliminate competition entirely," he said. The economists acknowledged that utility workers would be among the potential losers in the move toward competition. "Part of the efficiency is going to be releasing labor to other pursuits," said Crandall.
The study was funded by a group of low-cost utilities that are pushing for open power markets.

As lawmakers are bombarded by studies on the benefits of competition, the Electric Consumers' Alliance, including groups representing the elderly and poor, has disputed claims that they will gain from deregulation.
They fear that utilities will pass on their investment losses in the competitive market to small consumers as big industrial consumers switch to other power suppliers. -- Sonali Paul ((202 898 8320))
